expectedText:
COPYRIGHT ASSIGNMENT AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · Jordan Alex Lee

ASSIGNMENT OF COPYRIGHT
Jordan Alex Lee hereby assigns and transfers to Acme, Inc. all right, title, and interest in and to the copyright in the following work: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., including the exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, publicly display, publicly perform, and prepare derivative works based on it, for the full term of copyright and any renewals or extensions available under law. This assignment is effective as of the date this agreement is signed. Jordan Alex Lee agrees to sign any additional documents reasonably requested by Acme, Inc. to confirm, record, or perfect this assignment.

WHO OWNS THE WORK BEFORE IT'S ASSIGNED
Under federal copyright law, copyright in a work vests initially in the person who actually creates it — the author — the moment the work is fixed in a tangible form. When Jordan Alex Lee is an independent creator or freelancer rather than an employee of Acme, Inc., the employee branch of the work-made-for-hire doctrine does not apply, and Jordan Alex Lee is the initial copyright owner even though Acme, Inc. commissioned and paid for the work. Ownership passes to Acme, Inc. only through the assignment made in this agreement, or through one of the narrow work-made-for-hire exceptions described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Copyright in a work protected under this title vests initially in the author or authors of the work. The authors of a joint work are coowners of copyright in the work."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 201(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, initial ownership of copyright (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/201)
  "Absent an express transfer of ownership, a contributor who is not an employee retains ownership of his copyright."
  — Effects Associates, Inc. v. Cohen, 908 F.2d 555 (9th Cir. 1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/544754/effects-associates-inc-v-larry-cohen/)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how initial copyright ownership is allocated between an individual creator and a hiring party — not a claim that every commissioned work or every fact pattern is resolved the same way, since ownership can also be affected by joint-authorship rules, prior agreements, or other provisions of Title 17 not addressed here. The Effects Associates decision cited below is Ninth Circuit precedent; it is widely cited nationally on this point but is only binding within that circuit.

WHY MOST FREELANCE WORK ISN'T AUTOMATICALLY "WORK MADE FOR HIRE"
Federal copyright law defines “work made for hire” in two ways: (1) work created by an employee within the scope of employment, or (2) work that is both specially ordered or commissioned for use in one of nine specific categories listed in the statute — a contribution to a collective work, a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, or an atlas — and that the parties expressly agree in a signed written instrument is a work made for hire. Work by an independent creator like Jordan Alex Lee does not fall within the first branch, and most freelance deliverables — things like a logo, most illustration and graphic design, most software, most photography, and most website or marketing copy — do not fall within any of the nine categories in the second branch either. For work outside those categories, no work-made-for-hire designation in a contract can make Acme, Inc. the legal “author” of it; a separate written assignment, like this agreement, is what actually transfers ownership from Jordan Alex Lee to Acme, Inc.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A “work made for hire” is— (1) a work prepared by an employee within the scope of his or her employment; or (2) a work specially ordered or commissioned for use as a contribution to a collective work, as a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, as a translation, as a supplementary work, as a compilation, as an instructional text, as a test, as answer material for a test, or as an atlas, if the parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them that the work shall be considered a work made for hire."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of “work made for hire” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/101)
  "Nor was the sculpture a “work made for hire” under the second subsection of § 101 (hereinafter § 101(2)): sculpture is not one of the nine categories of works enumerated in that subsection, and the parties had not agreed in writing that the sculpture would be a work for hire."
  — Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730 (1989) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112273/community-for-creative-non-violence-v-reid/)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the statutory definition of “work made for hire” directly and confirms the nine enumerated categories by checking the statutory text itself, rather than assuming the count or the list. Whether a specific piece of work fits (or doesn't fit) one of those categories is a fact-specific characterization this clause doesn't resolve for any particular work. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the work-made-for-hire categories are defined — not a claim that every creative work, or every industry's customary way of describing its own output, has actually been tested against this list in litigation.

COPYRIGHT TRANSFERS MUST BE IN WRITING
Federal copyright law requires that a transfer of copyright ownership — other than by operation of law, such as through inheritance — be in a signed writing to be valid. An oral agreement, a handshake deal, or an implied understanding is generally not enough to transfer copyright ownership itself, even if it may create other rights (such as an implied license to use the work). This is part of why a signed assignment agreement like this one, rather than an invoice, a verbal agreement, or a course of dealing, is what's needed to actually move copyright ownership of A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. from Jordan Alex Lee to Acme, Inc.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner’s duly authorized agent."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, execution of transfers of copyright ownership (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/204)
  "The rule is really quite simple: If the copyright holder agrees to transfer ownership to another party, that party must get the copyright holder to sign a piece of paper saying so. It doesn't have to be the Magna Charta; a one-line pro forma statement will do."
  — Effects Associates, Inc. v. Cohen, 908 F.2d 555 (9th Cir. 1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/544754/effects-associates-inc-v-larry-cohen/)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the signed-writing requirement for copyright transfers — not a claim that every method of communicating agreement (email, a signed purchase order, electronic signature) satisfies it in every circumstance, which can depend on facts not addressed here. The cited Effects Associates decision is Ninth Circuit precedent; it is frequently cited nationally on this point but is only binding within that circuit.

THE STATUTORY RIGHT TO TERMINATE THIS ASSIGNMENT LATER
Assigning copyright ownership does not necessarily last forever, no matter what the assignment agreement says. Federal copyright law gives an individual author — or, after the author's death, certain statutorily defined heirs — the right to terminate a copyright transfer or license during a five-year window that begins 35 years after the grant was signed (or, for a grant covering publication rights, the earlier of 35 years from publication or 40 years from execution). This termination right exists notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, including language in the assignment itself purporting to waive it, but it does not apply to a work made for hire. To exercise it, the author or heirs must serve an advance written notice stating the effective termination date, served not less than two nor more than ten years before that date, and a copy of the notice must be recorded with the U.S. Copyright Office before termination takes effect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Termination of the grant may be effected at any time during a period of five years beginning at the end of thirty-five years from the date of execution of the grant; or, if the grant covers the right of publication of the work, the period begins at the end of thirty-five years from the date of publication of the work under the grant or at the end of forty years from the date of execution of the grant, whichever term ends earlier."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — timing (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  "The notice shall state the effective date of the termination, which shall fall within the five-year period specified by clause (3) of this subsection, and the notice shall be served not less than two or more than ten years before that date. A copy of the notice shall be recorded in the Copyright Office before the effective date of termination, as a condition to its taking effect."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — notice requirements (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  Known gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3) and § 203(a)(4)); no additional independent source was found for this, since both describe requirements of the same termination mechanism. The statute, by its own terms, applies only to a transfer or license “executed by the author on or after January 1, 1978” and expressly excludes a work made for hire — a status this document's other clauses address separately. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the termination right and its timing work — not a claim that any specific assignment made under this agreement will in fact be eligible for termination, since eligibility depends on facts (such as whether the party assigning the work is an individual human author, as opposed to, for example, a company, and when the assignment was signed) that this clause doesn't resolve.

MORAL RIGHTS ARE SEPARATE FROM COPYRIGHT OWNERSHIP
Separately from copyright ownership itself, federal law gives the author of certain “works of visual art” personal rights of attribution and integrity — the right to be credited (or not falsely credited) as the work's author, and the right to object to certain distortions, mutilations, or destruction of the work. These rights, sometimes called “moral rights,” belong to the individual human author and cannot be sold or transferred, even by an assignment like this one. They can only be waived, and only if the author expressly agrees to the waiver in a written instrument, signed by the author, that specifically identifies the work and the particular uses the waiver covers. Assigning copyright ownership of A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. to Acme, Inc. does not, by itself, waive any moral rights Jordan Alex Lee may have in it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The rights conferred by subsection (a) may not be transferred, but those rights may be waived if the author expressly agrees to such waiver in a written instrument signed by the author. Such instrument shall specifically identify the work, and uses of that work, to which the waiver applies, and the waiver shall apply only to the work and uses so identified."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 106A(e)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, rights of certain authors to attribution and integrity — transfer and waiver (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/106A)
  "A “work of visual art” is— (1) a painting, drawing, print, or sculpture, existing in a single copy, in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author... or (2) a still photographic image produced for exhibition purposes only, existing in a single copy that is signed by the author, or in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author. A work of visual art does not include— ...any merchandising item or advertising, promotional, descriptive, covering, or packaging material or container... (B) any work made for hire..."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of “work of visual art” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/101)
  Known gap: Moral rights under 17 U.S.C. § 106A apply only to a narrow statutory category called a “work of visual art” — in general, a single copy or a signed, numbered limited edition of 200 copies or fewer of a painting, drawing, print, or sculpture, or a still photograph produced for exhibition purposes only — and the definition expressly excludes posters, maps, applied art, most merchandising and advertising or promotional material, and any work made for hire. Most freelance deliverables (logos, software, written content, and most commercial illustration or photography) fall outside that definition and so are not affected by § 106A at all; this clause is included because it may be relevant to a narrower category of assigned work, not because it applies to every work this document could be used for. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how moral rights and their waiver requirements work under the one federal statute (the Visual Artists Rights Act) that creates them — not a claim that any particular work assigned under this agreement qualifies as a “work of visual art,” or that state-law moral-rights doctrines, which some states separately recognize, work the same way.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate agreement to the terms above.
